name: Corn Mazes
title: Corn Mazes Near Me — Find a Corn Maze in Your State
description: Find corn mazes near you. Browse farms with corn mazes across all 50 states, with addresses, hours, ratings and directions.
lede: The signature fall attraction. Find farms running corn mazes near you, from ten-minute kiddie loops to multi-acre puzzles that take an hour to solve.
intro:
A corn maze is cut into a standing field in late summer and stays open until the stalks are harvested, which is why most mazes open a week or two after the pumpkin patch itself and close hard at the end of the season. Size varies enormously — a small farm may cut a half-acre loop for children, while a destination farm cuts eight to twelve acres with checkpoints, a printed map and a punch card.

Two practical notes. First, most mazes close at dusk unless the farm runs a flashlight night, which is usually ticketed separately. Second, mazes are the first attraction shut down after heavy rain, because the paths turn to mud faster than anything else on the property. Call ahead if it has rained in the last 48 hours.
extraIntro: Not every maze is built for the same crowd. A half-acre loop with wide paths and no dead ends is a fine first maze for a four-year-old; an eight-acre puzzle with checkpoints and a punch card can genuinely take an adult group the better part of an hour to solve, and is a different day out entirely. If you're picking between a few options nearby, check the acreage and expected time on each listing below before you commit — it tells you more about who the maze is really for than the photos do.

faq.q: Is a corn maze good for adults, or just kids?
faq.a: Depends entirely on the maze. Small kiddie loops are built for young children and take ten to fifteen minutes; larger destination mazes cut eight to twelve acres with checkpoints and a printed map, and are genuinely challenging for adults. Check the size and estimated time on the listing before you go if you want a real puzzle.

faq.q: How long does a corn maze take to finish?
faq.a: Anywhere from ten minutes for a small children's loop to an hour or more for a large, multi-acre maze with checkpoints. Farms that run bigger mazes usually publish an estimated time on their own site — worth checking if you're planning around nap times or a tight schedule.

faq.q: What happens to a corn maze if it rains?
faq.a: It's usually the first attraction a farm closes. Cut paths through a standing field turn to mud faster than anything else on the property, so heavy rain in the last day or two is worth a call-ahead before you drive out.

faq.q: When do corn mazes open for the season?
faq.a: Typically a week or two after the pumpkin patch itself opens, since the maze needs to be cut into a fully grown standing field first. Most run through the end of October and close hard once the stalks are harvested — check the listing for a farm's specific dates.

name: U-Pick Pumpkin Patches
title: U-Pick Pumpkin Patches Near Me — Pick Your Own Pumpkins
description: Find pick-your-own pumpkin patches near you. Browse u-pick farms across all 50 states where you cut your own pumpkin straight from the vine.
lede: Cut your own pumpkin straight from the vine. These farms let you walk the field and pick, rather than choosing from a pile by the barn.
intro:
True u-pick means walking into a growing field and cutting a pumpkin off the vine yourself. It is the version of the experience most people picture, and it is worth checking for specifically — a great many farms advertised as pumpkin patches are actually display patches, where pumpkins are trucked in and arranged on straw for photographs.

Neither is wrong, but they are different days out. If cutting from the vine matters to you, call and ask directly whether the field is still open, particularly late in October when smaller growers pick out and switch to a pile.

Bring gloves and, ideally, your own shears. Vines are prickly, and a cleanly cut stem two to four inches long keeps a pumpkin fresh far longer than one twisted off by hand.
extraIntro: The clearest way to tell whether a farm is running a real u-pick field: ask on the phone whether you'll be cutting from the vine yourself, not just picking from a pile. Fields get picked out unevenly through the season — the biggest, most photogenic pumpkins tend to go first on opening weekends, while late October often means smaller pumpkins spread further apart. Neither is wrong, but if you're driving any real distance, a quick call about what's currently left in the field beats a wasted trip.

faq.q: What's the actual difference between u-pick and a regular pumpkin patch?
faq.a: True u-pick means walking into a growing field and cutting a pumpkin off the vine yourself. A regular or "display" patch trucks pumpkins in and arranges them on straw near the barn for you to choose from. Both are common, and it's worth calling ahead to ask which one a farm actually runs.

faq.q: Do I need to bring my own tools to pick a pumpkin?
faq.a: Gloves and, ideally, your own shears. Vines are prickly, and a cleanly cut stem two to four inches long keeps a pumpkin fresh far longer than one twisted off by hand. Some farms provide clippers at the field; many don't, so bring your own to be safe.

faq.q: Is u-pick more expensive than buying at the entrance?
faq.a: Usually the opposite — u-pick farms are commonly priced per pumpkin or by the pound with free entry, while flat-admission destination farms charge a gate fee on top of the pumpkin itself. A u-pick visit is often the cheapest version of this trip.

faq.q: When is the best time to go for the best selection?
faq.a: Early in the season, ideally the first two weekends after a farm opens, when the field hasn't been picked over. By late October, smaller growers frequently switch from true u-pick to a pre-picked pile once the field thins out — call ahead if cutting from the vine matters to you.

name: Hayrides
title: Hayrides Near Me — Find Farms With Hayrides and Wagon Rides
description: Find hayrides near you. Browse pumpkin patches and fall farms offering hayrides and tractor-drawn wagon rides across all 50 states.
lede: Tractor-drawn wagon rides out to the field and back. Often the whole point of the trip for younger children.
intro:
Hayrides run on a loop from the barn out to the pumpkin field, typically ten to twenty minutes, and at many farms they are the only way to reach the picking field at all. Some are free with admission, some are a few dollars a head, and at busy farms the wait can run half an hour on an October Saturday.

Evening haunted hayrides are a different attraction entirely — separately ticketed, age-restricted at many farms, and often genuinely intense. Do not assume a daytime wristband covers one.

Wagon rides stop when the ground is saturated. If you are travelling specifically for the hayride, a phone call after a wet spell will save you the drive.
extraIntro: Timing matters more for hayrides than almost any other attraction here. Weekday mornings mean walking straight onto a wagon; a mid-October Saturday afternoon can mean a thirty-minute line at a popular farm, since the tractor and wagon only hold so many people per trip. If a hayride is the main reason for your visit — especially with a toddler who won't wait well — go early in the day or midweek.

faq.q: Are hayrides free with admission?
faq.a: It varies by farm. Some include the hayride free with general admission, especially when it's the only way to reach the picking field; others charge a few dollars a head separately. Check the individual listing or call ahead if the price matters.

faq.q: What's the difference between a regular hayride and a haunted hayride?
faq.a: A regular hayride is a daytime tractor-drawn loop out to the pumpkin field, usually family-friendly and calm. A haunted hayride runs in the evening, is separately ticketed, and is often genuinely intense — don't assume a daytime wristband covers one.

faq.q: Do hayrides run when it's rained recently?
faq.a: Often not. Wagon rides stop when the ground is saturated, since a loaded wagon can't safely cross soft or muddy field paths. If you're travelling any distance specifically for the hayride, a quick call after a wet spell is worth it.

faq.q: How long does a hayride usually last?
faq.a: Typically ten to twenty minutes each way, though it varies by farm and how far the picking field sits from the barn. At some farms it's the only route out to the pumpkins; at others it's a standalone attraction you can skip.

name: Haunted Attractions
title: Haunted Attractions Near Me — Haunted Hayrides, Mazes and Trails
description: Find haunted attractions near you: haunted hayrides, haunted corn mazes and haunted trails at farms across all 50 states.
lede: Haunted hayrides, haunted corn mazes and haunted trails, run by working farms after dark.
intro:
Farm haunts run in the evening, usually Friday and Saturday from late September, and they are ticketed separately from daytime admission almost everywhere. Intensity varies far more than at a commercial haunted house: some are mild walk-throughs suitable for ten-year-olds, others involve chainsaws, actors who follow you, and a minimum age.

Ask two questions before booking for a family: what age the farm recommends, and whether actors make contact. The answers differ from farm to farm and are rarely published clearly.

Expect queues on the two weekends before Halloween, and check whether tickets are timed — many farms have moved to timed entry to control the lines.
extraIntro: A farm haunt is a genuinely different business than a commercial haunted house chain — it's a working pumpkin patch that repurposes its own corn maze, hayride or trail after dark, often with local volunteer or seasonal actors rather than a professional scare-actor crew. That's usually a point in its favor (lower prices, a shorter and more personal walk-through), but it also means the intensity and polish vary far more farm to farm than a big commercial haunt would. Reviews mentioning specific attractions — the haunted hayride versus the walk-through trail — are worth reading before you pick one for a group with mixed comfort levels.

faq.q: Are haunted attractions included with daytime pumpkin patch admission?
faq.a: Almost never. Haunted hayrides, haunted corn mazes and haunted trails run in the evening on a separate ticket from daytime admission, and frequently require a different visit entirely rather than the same trip.

faq.q: What age are farm haunted attractions appropriate for?
faq.a: It varies far more than at a commercial haunted house. Some are mild walk-throughs suitable for ten-year-olds; others involve actors who follow or make contact, and carry a recommended minimum age. Ask the farm directly before booking for a family with young kids.

faq.q: When do haunted attractions run?
faq.a: Typically evenings only, Friday and Saturday from late September through Halloween weekend — separate from the farm's regular daytime pumpkin-patch hours. Check the listing or the farm's own site for its current haunt schedule.

faq.q: Do I need to buy tickets in advance?
faq.a: Many farms have moved to timed entry specifically to control lines, especially on the two weekends before Halloween when queues run longest. If a specific night matters to you, buying ahead is the safer move.

name: Petting Zoos and Farm Animals
title: Pumpkin Patches With Petting Zoos Near Me — Farm Animals for Kids
description: Find pumpkin patches with petting zoos and farm animals near you. Ideal for toddlers and preschoolers, across all 50 states.
lede: Goats, sheep, alpacas and barn cats. The attraction that reliably holds a three-year-old's attention longer than the pumpkins do.
intro:
For families with toddlers and preschoolers, an animal barn is often worth more than every other attraction on the farm combined. Most are included with admission; feed cups usually cost a dollar or two.

Two things worth knowing. Hand-washing stations are required at well-run farms and are worth using properly — animal contact areas are a recognised source of E. coli and salmonella exposure in young children. And strollers are frequently not permitted inside animal enclosures, so plan for carrying.
extraIntro: If a petting zoo is the actual reason for the trip — not just a bonus stop — go earlier in the day. Animals get fed and are more active in the morning, and feed cups sometimes run out by afternoon on a busy Saturday. It's also worth checking the listing for what kind of animals a farm actually keeps: a small barn with a few goats and rabbits is a very different stop than a larger farm running alpacas, a mini-horse or an aviary alongside the usual sheep and barn cats.

faq.q: Is the petting zoo included in general admission?
faq.a: At most farms, yes — the animal barn is bundled into general admission rather than ticketed separately. It's still worth confirming when you call, since a minority of larger destination farms do charge extra for it.

faq.q: What animals will actually be there?
faq.a: It varies by farm, but goats, sheep, alpacas, rabbits and barn cats are the most common. Larger farms sometimes add pigs, ponies or a small aviary. Check the individual listing for specifics where we have them.

faq.q: Are petting zoos safe for toddlers?
faq.a: Generally yes, with normal precautions. Well-run farms provide hand-washing stations near the animal area — worth using properly, since animal contact areas are a recognized source of E. coli and salmonella exposure in young children. Strollers are frequently not permitted inside the enclosure itself, so plan for carrying.

faq.q: Do I need to bring anything, or pay extra to feed the animals?
faq.a: Feed cups are usually available on site for a dollar or two, even when general admission is free or already paid. You don't need to bring your own animal feed, and farms generally don't allow outside food for the animals.

name: Apple Picking
title: Apple Picking Near Me — Orchards With Pumpkin Patches
description: Find farms combining apple picking and pumpkin patches near you. Pick apples and pumpkins in the same trip, across all 50 states.
lede: Farms where you can pick apples and pumpkins in the same trip — usually the best value fall outing there is.
intro:
Orchards that also run a pumpkin patch give you the longest season of any farm type: apples start in August in most regions and run through October, overlapping the pumpkin window entirely. Pricing is normally by the bag or the peck rather than per apple.

Ask which varieties are ready on the day you visit. Orchards rotate blocks through the season, and turning up for Honeycrisp two weeks after that block is picked out is the most common disappointment at apple farms.

Cider and cider donuts are usually made on site at these farms, and are the main reason many people return.
extraIntro: Because apple season runs so much longer than pumpkin season, an orchard-plus-pumpkin-patch farm is worth visiting twice — once in September for apples at their peak, and again in October once the pumpkin field and any corn maze or hayride are fully running. Calling ahead to ask which apple varieties are currently being picked is the single most useful question, since a farm's own site or listing rarely updates that in real time.

faq.q: Can I pick apples and pumpkins on the same trip?
faq.a: Yes, at farms that run both — the two seasons overlap for most of September and October, so a single visit can cover both. Check the listing for which attractions a specific farm actually offers before you go.

faq.q: How is apple picking usually priced?
faq.a: By the bag or by the peck rather than per apple, at most farms. Exact pricing isn't something we track directly, since it changes farm to farm and year to year — call ahead or check the farm's own site to confirm current rates.

faq.q: How do I know which apple varieties will be ready?
faq.a: Ask the farm directly on the day you're planning to visit. Orchards rotate through different blocks as the season goes on, and arriving after a specific variety like Honeycrisp has been picked out is the most common disappointment — farms don't always update this online in real time.

faq.q: When does apple picking season start?
faq.a: Typically August in most regions, running through October — a longer window than pumpkin season, which usually doesn't open until mid-to-late September. That overlap is what makes combined apple-and-pumpkin farms worth two separate visits.

name: Sunflower Fields
title: Sunflower Fields Near Me — U-Pick Sunflowers and Photo Fields
description: Find sunflower fields near you at pumpkin patches and fall farms across all 50 states. U-pick stems and photo sessions.
lede: Photo fields and u-pick stems, usually peaking a few weeks before the pumpkins do.
intro:
Sunflower fields have become a fixture at fall farms, and they run on a much tighter schedule than pumpkins. A planting is at peak for roughly ten to fourteen days, after which the heads droop and the field is cut. Farms almost always post bloom updates — check before you drive out, because a week either side of peak is a materially different photograph.

Most fields charge a small entry fee plus a per-stem price for cutting. Professional photography is frequently restricted or separately ticketed; clear it in advance if you are bringing a photographer.
extraIntro: Because the bloom window is so short, a sunflower field is the one attraction on this site worth checking the same week you plan to go, not just the same season. Many farms post bloom-status updates on social media or their own site rather than keeping a page updated year-round, so a quick search for the farm's name plus "sunflower update" often turns up more current information than a general listing can.

faq.q: When do sunflower fields actually bloom?
faq.a: It varies by farm and region, but sunflower fields typically peak a few weeks before pumpkin season is in full swing, and stay at peak for only about ten to fourteen days before the heads droop. Check the farm's own site or social media for current bloom status before you drive out.

faq.q: Is there a fee just to walk the field?
faq.a: Most fields charge a small entry fee, plus a separate per-stem price if you want to cut your own flowers. Exact pricing isn't something we track directly — confirm with the farm before you go.

faq.q: Can I cut my own sunflowers to take home?
faq.a: At most u-pick sunflower fields, yes, usually for a per-stem price on top of the entry fee. Some fields are photo-only with cutting not permitted — check the individual listing or call ahead if taking flowers home matters to you.

faq.q: Are professional photos allowed in the field?
faq.a: Frequently restricted or ticketed separately from general admission — sunflower fields are popular for engagement and family photos, and many farms now charge a session fee for anyone bringing a professional camera or a planned photo shoot. Clear it with the farm in advance.

name: Fall Festivals
title: Fall Festivals Near Me — Harvest and Pumpkin Festivals
description: Find fall festivals and harvest events at farms near you, with live music, food, crafts and pumpkin patches, across all 50 states.
lede: Harvest weekends with live music, food stalls, craft vendors and everything the farm runs, all going at once.
intro:
A festival weekend is the farm operating at full capacity: every attraction open, food vendors on site, live music, and frequently craft or produce markets. It is the best day to visit if you want the complete experience, and the worst day to visit if you want a quiet field and a short queue.

Festival dates are usually a handful of specific weekends rather than the whole season, and they are the days farms are most likely to charge a higher gate price or require advance tickets. Confirm the date directly with the farm — festival schedules change year to year more than regular hours do.
extraIntro: Think of a fall festival weekend as the farm's version of a grand opening, repeated a few times a season rather than every day. If your priority is genuinely experiencing everything a farm runs — corn maze, hayride, live music, food vendors, craft stalls — a festival date is the day to go. If you'd rather have a shorter line at the corn maze and a quieter field for photos, a regular weekday or early weekend morning outside a festival date is the better call.

faq.q: What's actually included at a fall festival?
faq.a: Everything the farm runs, all at once: the corn maze, hayride and pumpkin patch alongside live music, food vendors, and often a craft or produce market. It's the farm operating at full capacity rather than a separate, smaller event.

faq.q: Do fall festivals cost more than a regular visit?
faq.a: Often, yes. Festival weekends are the days a farm is most likely to charge a higher gate price or require advance tickets, since every attraction is running. Confirm current pricing directly with the farm — it changes year to year more than regular admission does.

faq.q: When are fall festival weekends usually held?
faq.a: Typically a handful of specific weekends in the back half of the season, rather than the whole season — often concentrated in October. Exact dates vary farm to farm and change year to year, so check the farm's own site directly before planning a trip around one.

faq.q: Is a fall festival the same as a regular pumpkin patch visit?
faq.a: Not quite. A regular visit gets you the pumpkin patch and whichever attractions run daily; a festival weekend adds live music, food vendors and craft or produce markets on top, and is usually busier and sometimes pricier as a result.
